summary: If you were raised with Christ — seek the things above, where Christ is, where your true life is hidden with him in God until the day both are revealed in glory. Therefore: put to death the earthly members — the lusts that put them on the rubbish heap before; put off the old man's sins of speech and temper; put on the new man being renewed after the Creator's image — where Christ is all and in all, erasing the old labels of people. Then the assembly's uniform: compassion, kindness, humility, patience — bearing with each other, forgiving as the Lord forgave, love as the bond. The peace of God rules; the word of Christ dwells richly; everything is done in Jesus's name with thanksgiving. Finally the household lists: wives, husbands, children, fathers, servants, each addressed in turn.
whyItMatters: This chapter translates the whole letter's cosmic claims into clothes and kitchen talk — stripped and re-clothed identity, the community's peace governed by Christ, then the most concrete scratch test of the raised life: how wives, husbands, children, fathers, and servants function. The letter's theology ends in the same four walls as its rival teaching worked in.

context.author: Paul, in instruction-mode — the 'if...then' of 3:1-4 claims a fact about them and draws the floor-plan of the new life.
context.audience: Adults of a mixed household assembly — men, women, parents, children, slaves (3:18-4:1) — approached directly by name and station.
context.date: Undated; the chapter's horizon is God's disclosure day: 'When Christ, our life, is revealed, then you will also be revealed with him in glory' (3:4).
context.setting: A Roman household — the normal unit of work and worship — under pressure from rules that skip the household for the heavenly temple; the chapter answers by keeping the raised life domestic.
context.literaryForm: A four-verse theological platform ('if... then seek the things above'), two vice lists, two virtue lists, a rule for peace and worship, then a parallel household code — each move the same verb: put off / put on.

outline.heading: The if-then platform
outline.note: Raised people seek the things above, where Christ is — their life hidden with Christ in God, awaiting joint revelation in glory.

outline.heading: Put to death the earthly members
outline.note: The list of earth-born sins to kill: immorality, covetousness which is idolatry — the things for which wrath comes. Anger, wrath, malice, slander, shameful speech, lies — they dropped the old man with his deeds. Once they lived in these; no longer.

outline.heading: Put on the new man — the Creator's image
outline.note: The new self being renewed in knowledge after the image of its Creator — where there is no Greek and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, barbarian, Scythian, bondman, freeman — but Christ is all and in all.

outline.heading: The assembly's uniform
outline.note: Compassion, kindness, lowliness, meekness, patience; bearing with one another, forgiving as the Lord forgave; above all love, which binds perfection; let the peace of God rule, be thankful, let Christ's word dwell richly, sing with grace, and do everything in Jesus's name.

outline.heading: The household pairs (first four)
outline.note: Wives subject to husbands as fitting in the Lord; husbands love and do not become bitter; children obey in all things; fathers do not provoke; servants obey from the heart whatever they do as to the Lord — knowing the inheritance is received from the Lord Christ, whose paymasters do not show favoritism.

keyVerses.text: For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
keyVerses.why: The letter's interior rendering of conversion: the death and hiding are past, the revelation still awaits; the chapter's practical instructions stand on this fact.

keyVerses.text: where there can’t be Greek and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, barbarian, Scythian, bondservant, or free person; but Christ is all, and in all.
keyVerses.why: The letter's boundary-erasing clause — the world's labels disappear 'where' (the new man); Christ is both all there is and in everyone.

keyVerses.text: Above all these things, walk in love, which is the bond of perfection.
keyVerses.why: The layered instruction has a peak: love is the connector of the whole outfit — the garment over the virtues that holds them together.

themes: one in Christ beyond the labels
love that holds the virtues together

questions.question: Why 'seek the things above' rather than 'be heavenly-minded'?
questions.answer: The instruction names the location — where Christ is seated at God's right hand — and the mind-direction that follows: set your thoughts there, not on earthly things (3:1-2). The point is not disembodiment, as the chapter shows when it immediately commands the earthly members to be put to death: the above-things are a position that governs ordinary treatment of speech, temper, relationships, work.

questions.question: Why does Paul say our life 'is hidden with Christ in God'?
questions.answer: The verbs are past and present: you died (then), your life is hidden (now — settled, secured) (3:3). The condition of obscurity includes visible weakness, mistreatment, and the world's lack of applause, all read as the hidden stage before disclosure: 'when Christ, our life, is revealed, then you will also be revealed with him in glory' (3:4).

questions.question: What does 'mortify' or 'put to death' your members mean?
questions.answer: The instruction is total, not cosmetic — the earthly members are listed: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, 'which is idolatry' (3:5). The members noun is the body only in the sense of life-habits through it (3:5); killing here is not self-harm but terminating an operation, the way a servant is dismissed from service. Once they lived in these things; no longer.

questions.question: Why is covetousness called idolatry?
questions.answer: Because idols are covetousness made visible — the thing we want becomes the thing we bend knee to (3:5). Paul names economics among the constituents of an idolatrous heart rather than a morally neutral desire.

questions.question: Why 'there is no Greek and Jew... Scythian, slave, free'?
questions.answer: The list goes beyond the letter's usual Jew-Gentile line to include the language extremes (barbarian), remotest enemy (Scythian), and the law's fixed statuses (slave, free) (3:11). In the new person, Christ is all and in all — the particular distinctions that structured the old ranking lose their claim. The letter is not saying the differences ceased visibly; it is saying they can't mark anything that matters.

questions.question: How does one 'put on' compassion and kindness?
questions.answer: The same verbs as for taking off fit clothing — put on (3:12) — because virtues here are garments, the visible layer others interact with. Each is chosen: a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, patience. The seal is love as the bond (3:14), and the safeguards are peace's rule and Christ's word dwelling richly, with corporate singing as the normal oxygen (3:15-16).

questions.question: Why do wives get a shorter instruction than husbands?
questions.answer: The single-instruction allocation mirrors the household power distribution: wives in the Roman household owed obedience (3:18) while the husband commands love — the larger demand (3:19). The pairs are not symmetrical in volume because the danger was not symmetrical; the instruction is sieved through the same theological sieve as the whole letter — fitting in the Lord for wives, not bitter for husbands — and both sides have their behavior cordoned off by a higher sovereignty.

questions.question: Does 'servants, obey...' tell slaves to accept their condition?
questions.answer: The instruction addresses the person inside the institution with dignity and boundaries: service is heartfelt, as to the Lord rather than merely when watched, and their ultimate paymaker — the inheritance — comes from the Lord Christ (3:22-24). Verse 25 then balances for everyone: wrongdoers get what is coming, without partiality. The letter navigates reality without rewriting the economy; its slave-and-master passage pairs with the explicit no-favorites line to keep the elevated status of the enslaved in view.

questions.question: If they 'died' (3:3), why does verse 5 tell them to put their members to death?
questions.answer: The chapter holds a deliberate tension: they 'died' with Christ already (3:3), and yet certain earthly members still need killing (3:5). The resolution is the letter's standing pattern — the finished state and the unfinished walk are both true at once: 'you died' settles their identity and location, 'put to death' is the daily enforcement of it. Dying to the old self is not the same as being its victim again; the first verdict has to be worked out.

glossary.def: The believer's present condition: real, secure, invisible to the world; the life is preserved in God's custody until its disclosure with Christ (3:3-4).
The letter's word for finishing a former habit — termination of an operation, not physique (3:5).
The garment worn over the other virtues that keeps them tied together (3:14); the letter's summary of how all the 'put on' pieces hold.
